sketches.title: The Letter Gets Worse
sketches.premise: You and a rival write one complaint letter, adding one paragraph per turn. Start with a real annoyance; each new paragraph must make the complaint cause a fresh, believable problem while the host hypes the disaster and roasts weak writing.
sketches.criterion: The judge checks that the paragraph follows from the whole letter, adds one new event or consequence, does not skip from a small gripe to a final catastrophe, does not solve or close the complaint, does not undo a fact, and is not merely an insult, feeling, or unrelated rant.
sketches.move_shape: Write one paragraph beginning with “Then,” naming one new consequence caused by the letter so far; example: “Then the building manager posts our complaint on the lobby board, so every neighbor now knows we blamed the night-shift cleaner.”
sketches.first_card: Dear Building Manager: The lobby vending machine charged me twice for one bag of chips, and the refund button is missing.

sketches.title: Exhibit A, Unfortunately
sketches.premise: You and a rival build a complaint letter by adding one paragraph each, but every paragraph must introduce a new piece of evidence. The host calls each receipt, photo, witness, or strange detail like a courtroom announcer and mocks anyone whose proof is flimsy.
sketches.criterion: The judge checks that each paragraph adds one specific new piece of evidence caused or revealed by the standing complaint, fits every earlier claim, does not leap to a verdict or punishment, does not erase evidence, and is not just anger, a conclusion, or a repeated receipt.
sketches.move_shape: Add one paragraph beginning with “Then,” presenting one new checkable exhibit and explaining how it supports the letter; example: “Then I checked the timestamp on the receipt and found three charges in the same minute, all from the machine beside the broken camera.”
sketches.first_card: Dear Customer Service: Your café charged me for a plain sandwich, but the receipt lists an item called “premium mystery filling.”

sketches.title: CC Everyone
sketches.premise: You and a rival write a complaint one paragraph at a time, and each paragraph must widen the audience who receives, reads, or reacts to it. The host cheers every accidental leak and delivers savage commentary when the letter reaches someone who should absolutely not be reading it.
sketches.criterion: The judge checks that each paragraph follows from the letter’s current sharing trail, adds one new recipient or public reaction, keeps the complaint itself active, does not jump past likely readers, does not end with a final response, does not undo a sent copy, and is not only a mood or insult.
sketches.move_shape: Add one paragraph beginning with “Then,” naming one new person or group who gets the letter and one immediate reaction; example: “Then the receptionist forwards it to the company chat, where the security guard asks why his lunch is now part of the evidence.”
sketches.first_card: Dear Train Company: Your 8:10 train left two minutes early, while I was standing beside the open door waving like an idiot.

sketches.title: Please See Rule 47
sketches.premise: You and a rival grow a complaint letter by adding one paragraph each, and every paragraph uncovers a new rule, form, fee, or office needed to handle the complaint. The host acts like a delighted tour guide through useless red tape and roasts every fresh bureaucratic trap.
sketches.criterion: The judge checks that each new rule or office is a plain consequence of the current complaint process, fits the whole letter, does not skip several required steps, does not grant a final fix, does not cancel an earlier rule, and is not just a complaint about paperwork.
sketches.move_shape: Add one paragraph beginning with “Then,” naming the next required step and why the letter has triggered it; example: “Then the help desk says a double-charge complaint needs Form 9B, signed by a witness who watched the machine swallow the second payment.”
sketches.first_card: Dear Apartment Office: The laundry room ate my last coin, and the washing machine still shows “waiting.”

sketches.title: Sorry About Your Sorry
sketches.premise: You and a rival build one complaint letter by adding a paragraph that changes who answers and what they claim happened. Each reply must create a new problem for the letter, while the host hypes every fake apology and savages corporate word soup.
sketches.criterion: The judge checks that each paragraph is a believable reply caused by the standing complaint, adds one new claim or demand that creates the next issue, fits all earlier replies, does not skip straight to a final settlement, does not retract or rewrite a reply, and is not only a feeling or insult.
sketches.move_shape: Add one paragraph beginning with “Then,” giving the next reply and the new snag it creates; example: “Then the manager apologizes for the ‘temporary smell’ but says the room is safe, even though her note quietly asks us not to mention the leaking ceiling.”
sketches.first_card: Dear Cinema Manager: The seat I booked was covered by a paper sign, and the usher told me to sit somewhere else after the film began.

sketches.title: Dear Internet, It’s Me Again
sketches.premise: You and a rival grow a complaint letter paragraph by paragraph as the writer tries to post it online. Each paragraph must cause a new public reaction, remix, or reply that changes the complaint’s path; the host provides chaotic hype and a sharp roast for every cursed comment.
sketches.criterion: The judge checks that each paragraph follows from the complaint’s current online spread, adds one new post, reply, image, or reaction with a clear cause, does not skip from posting to total fame or ruin, does not end the thread, does not delete or undo a post, and is not merely a rant or moral.
sketches.move_shape: Add one paragraph beginning with “Then,” describing one new online response caused by the latest post and the concrete problem it creates; example: “Then a local account reposts the photo, but its caption says the shop is giving away free phones, so strangers start lining up outside.”
sketches.first_card: Dear Corner Shop: Your self-checkout called my apple “unexpected,” then locked the whole machine while I stood there holding fruit like evidence.
